lead.kicker: Ajay Shah on why India should love foreign investment
lead.head: A love letter to foreign capital

pic.caption: Ajay Shah (left) and Amit Varma early in Episode 111

body: Amit Varma promised his gen­tle read­ers an episode not about money but about love. Ajay Shah, he said, had con­fided that he has five great loves. {111-J01}
Shah named firm pro­duc­tiv­ity, cap­i­tal ac­count open­ness and in­fla­tion tar­get­ing. The fifth, and the sub­ject of the hour, was for­eign di­rect in­vest­ment.

Their first meet­ing came in the early 1980s, when an American from Corning Glass vis­ited Shah’s fa­ther, hop­ing to build a glass fac­tory in India. The fa­ther told him the Indian state would not allow it.
Shah called the sub­ject “a crit­i­cal bat­tle­front” for the next 25 years of the Indian story, and no been-there, done-that topic.
## An hon­est es­cape valve

The heart of his case was a dream. A coun­try ad­mits that its in­sti­tu­tions are bad, and walls off a patch of land, say one square kilo­me­tre, where for­eign fac­to­ries are spared local labour law, tax ha­rass­ment, visa trou­ble and cus­toms du­ties.
“It takes enor­mous hon­esty to say this openly,” Shah said.
The state gives up its depre­da­tions. In ex­change, thou­sands of work­ers get jobs, and the state col­lects in­come tax on their wages and GST on their spend­ing.
That, he ar­gued, was the great­ness of the Chinese model under Deng Xiaoping: FDI into China ran under good in­sti­tu­tions, be­cause the state was able to back off. {111-C03}
The big­ger prize is knowl­edge. Workers in for­eign firms learn the global fron­tier of pro­duc­tiv­ity, then move to other jobs or start firms of their own, tak­ing it with them.

India, Shah said, never said these para­graphs to it­self clearly. Talk of a level play­ing field misses the point. The bar­gain only works if for­eign firms es­cape what Indian reg­u­la­tors, cap­i­tal con­trols and visa rules do to ev­ery­one else. {111-C05}
“If there is a magic in FDI, it is Deng Xiaoping,” he said.

Varma stressed that this is no ar­gu­ment against fix­ing India’s in­sti­tu­tions, a fight that will go on. Meanwhile, “lit­tle is­lands of free­dom” are worth hav­ing: “let’s not let the per­fect be the enemy of the good.”
## The money that can leave
Indian pol­icy cir­cles treat FDI as the good guy and port­fo­lio in­vest­ment as hot money. Shah said that view comes “from a place of deep in­se­cu­rity”, and is an­a­lyt­i­cally wrong.
Foreigners al­ready know India’s weak­nesses and price them in, he said, and India has never had a big cri­sis from for­eign port­fo­lio exit.

Contrary to many Indian econ­o­mists, he ar­gued, port­fo­lio in­vest­ment needs bet­ter in­sti­tu­tions than FDI does: trust­wor­thy ac­counts, au­dits, a stock mar­ket and a de­pos­i­tory. {111-C07}

The re­sis­tance is po­lit­i­cal. Portfolio money gives Indian busi­ness more buy­ers for its shares and a lower cost of cap­i­tal; FDI gives it com­pe­ti­tion. Shah cred­ited that in­sight to Ila Patnaik.
## A rare win­dow

Shah closed on hope. The break­down of the China model and America’s tur­moil over tar­iffs have re­shaped the world econ­omy. The surge is not yet in the data, he ad­mit­ted, but the con­di­tions are right.
“I think 2025 is an im­por­tant mo­ment in India’s his­tory,” he said. {111-C13}
Varma had the last word. “And if it doesn’t hap­pen, we are play­ing a long game.”

second.label: Investment treaties
second.head: Insured by a slap
second.deck: Ajay Shah on why India should compensate the investors it expropriates

pic.caption: Ajay Shah on investment treaties as insurance

body: Foreign in­vestors need a pre­dictable en­vi­ron­ment, Amit Varma said, not the “ret­ro­spec­tive tax­a­tion kind of non­sense” done to Vodafone. {#vodafone} Ajay Shah’s an­swer is the bi­lat­eral in­vest­ment treaty, in which India prom­ises to com­pen­sate for­eign in­vestors when­ever any level of the Indian state ex­pro­pri­ates them.

Paying out $1 bil­lion a year to sta­bilise $100 bil­lion of FDI is a good deal, Shah said, like an in­sur­ance pre­mium. {#insurance} And a slap in the face each time the state mis­be­haves is how checks and bal­ances get built. {111-C10}

But of­fi­cials who lost cases took them per­son­ally, and a machismo set in. A new model treaty in 2016 aban­doned many good ideas. {#modelbit} Today, Shah said, India is in­creas­ingly hos­tile to such treaties.

quote.text: It’s ac­tu­ally bril­liantly in­cen­tive com­pat­i­ble for the Indian state to pay money when the Indian state mis­be­haves.

third.head: Too proud to stoop

pic.caption: Ajay Shah on India’s anti-foreigner streak

body: India’s dis­trust of for­eign cap­i­tal runs deep, Ajay Shah said. “There is a deep anti-foreigner streak in India. There is a deep anti-Western streak in India.” In deep ways, he added, it has fed into Indian fail­ure. {111-C11}

There is also a cult of third-worldism, in which multi­na­tion­als be­came a bad word. In its old pic­ture, he said, poor help­less Bengali work­ers are ex­ploited in a Texas Instruments fac­tory. {#texas}

A newer ar­ro­gance has joined it: India is so im­por­tant that for­eign com­pa­nies have no choice but to come, so why stoop? Development goes well, Shah said, when pol­i­cy­mak­ers hon­estly pur­sue growth, and badly when pride creeps in.
Amit Varma blamed a toxic, in­su­lar na­tion­al­ism of the we-don’t-need-the-world kind. “All trade, all human con­nec­tion is pos­i­tive sum,” he said.

p2.title: Foreign affairs
p2.deck: Ajay Shah’s argument for foreign direct investment, chapter by chapter, with Amit Varma asking the questions

from1.head: A love letter to foreign capital

quote.text: If you say FDI, you’re a pro­pa­gan­dist. Okay, you have to be pre­cise.

box.title: Deng Xiaoping’s honest bargain
box.text: Deng Xiaoping, Ajay Shah said, saw that fix­ing China’s Companies Act and GST would take a hun­dred years. So he built a trusted, pre­dictable in­ter­face for for­eign­ers in the mean­time. His dream, Shah joked, was that there would be no Xi Jinping. {111-J02}

sections.label: First principles
sections.head: Ten per cent, seven numbers
sections.caption: what counts as FDI
body: Loosely, we think of FDI as a for­eigner build­ing a fac­tory in India. Ajay Shah’s def­i­ni­tion is tighter: a for­eigner hold­ing a sub­stan­tial, long-term stake in an Indian pro­duc­tion ar­range­ment. Buy shares in an Indian bak­ery com­pany such as Britannia and sell them next week, and that is port­fo­lio in­vest­ment.
Where is the line? The OECD and the IMF have agreed on a min­i­mum eq­uity hold­ing of 10 per cent. At 9 per cent, it is not FDI. {111-C01}

Other things count too. A for­eign parent’s loan to its Indian sub­sidiary is FDI. So is a for­eign pri­vate eq­uity fund’s 11 per cent stake in a com­pletely Indian com­pany, though that both­ers some peo­ple. Profits a for­eign-owned op­er­a­tion rein­vests in India, rather than repa­tri­at­ing, are booked as a brand new FDI flow that year.
## A menu for pro­pa­gan­dists

The bal­ance of pay­ments gives “beau­ti­ful, trusted, high qual­ity” data, Shah said. But there are seven num­bers: gross in­flow, repa­tri­a­tion and net for FDI in India, the match­ing three for FDI by India, and a “net net” over­all. {#seven}

Propagandists of every stripe pick which­ever flat­ters their story. Shah’s surest sign of pro­pa­ganda is a chart ti­tled sim­ply “FDI”. Proper la­belling, he com­plained, is miss­ing “fifty per cent of the time, sev­enty per cent of the time”. {111-C02}
~ Amit Varma was suit­ably chas­tened. “I’m never gonna say FDI in front of you again,” he said. {111-J03}

quote.text: If you say FDI, you’re a pro­pa­gan­dist. Okay, you have to be pre­cise.

sections.label: The dream
sections.head: One square kilometre of sanity
sections.caption: the dream of FDI
body: Picture a coun­try with bad in­sti­tu­tions, Ajay Shah said, that gets it­self to­gether just enough to say: for this one square kilo­me­tre, build your fac­tory and you will be pro­tected from the depre­da­tions of the local in­sti­tu­tions. {#squarekm}

No local labour law, no mess­ing with tax­a­tion, no visa trou­ble, no cus­toms du­ties on goods com­ing in or going out. The clean­est form is a bonded ware­house, where im­ports ar­rive fully ex­empt and fin­ished goods leave for the world. {#bonded}
The state gives up its depre­da­tions. In re­turn, thou­sands of work­ers get jobs, and it col­lects in­come tax on their wages and GST on their spend­ing.
## Deng’s bar­gain

This was the great­ness of the Chinese and South East Asian model. Deng Xiaoping’s China ac­cepted that fix­ing its Companies Act and GST would take a hun­dred years, and would not hold its breath. {#hundredyears}
The sec­ond prize is knowl­edge. People in for­eign firms learn the global fron­tier of pro­duc­tiv­ity, then leave to work for other com­pa­nies or start their own. {111-C04}
~ India, Shah said, never said these para­graphs to it­self clearly enough, and that is why FDI here has never quite worked out well.

quote.text: FDI into China op­er­ates under good in­sti­tu­tions be­cause the Chinese state is able to back off.

sections.label: The other money
sections.head: Hot money, cool heads
sections.caption: portfolio investment
body: In Indian pol­icy cir­cles, FDI is the good guy and port­fo­lio in­vest­ment is hot money that can buy today and sell to­mor­row. Ajay Shah traced the fear to in­se­cu­rity: a port­fo­lio in­vestor can sell and leave, and that fright­ens an in­se­cure Indian. {111-C06}
His ad­vice came from love: “If you love some­thing, set it free. If it comes back, it is yours. If it doesn’t, it never was.” {111-J05}

The fear is also an­a­lyt­i­cally wrong, he said. Foreigners al­ready know India’s weak­nesses, and those are priced in. Foreign in­vestors are no mono­lith: every day brings large gross buy­ing and sell­ing and a tiny net. And when shocks like the COVID lock­down come, Indians and for­eign­ers sell alike. {#covid}
## Paper you can trust

In fact, Shah ar­gued, port­fo­lio in­vest­ment needs bet­ter in­sti­tu­tions than FDI does. {111-C07} A fac­tory needs only a state that backs off and “three pages of rules”. An in­vestor in Tokyo, handed a piece of paper say­ing he owns a thou­sand shares of Reliance, needs trust­wor­thy ac­counts, audit, a stock mar­ket and a de­pos­i­tory.
That is why China never got port­fo­lio in­vest­ment going, Shah said, while India, with a hun­dred and fifty years of ac­count­ing tra­di­tion, can. {#accounting}
~ Who, he asked, is any econ­o­mist to call one flow good and an­other bad? Private peo­ple should de­cide; the government’s job is to build in­sti­tu­tions.

quote.text: It is FDI that de­mands a lower in­sti­tu­tional qual­ity and FPI de­mands a higher in­sti­tu­tional qual­ity.

sections.label: Who wants what
sections.head: Buyers welcome, rivals not
sections.caption: the politics of foreign money
body: If the eco­nom­ics is so clear, Amit Varma asked, why does the con­sen­sus run the other way? Ajay Shah’s an­swer turned on who gains.

A for­eigner with a fac­tory in India will want to sell in India too. A for­eigner mak­ing cars hurts Premier Padmini; Indian re­tail is angry at Amazon and Walmart. For the Indian rich, FDI means com­pe­ti­tion. {111-C08}

Portfolio money is the op­po­site: more buy­ers for their shares and bonds, and a lower cost of cap­i­tal. Shah cred­ited the in­sight to Ila Patnaik. Varma summed it up: “On one side of the de­bate you have se­cu­ri­ties. On the other side you have in­se­cu­ri­ties.” {111-J06}

A pure ex­port en­clave, Shah thought, would be po­lit­i­cally harm­less; it has failed for want of in­tel­lec­tual clar­ity. India has an SEZ Act of 2005, but never im­mu­nised for­eign firms from Indian in­sti­tu­tions. {#sez2005}
## Behind the tar­iff wall

Trade bar­ri­ers bring a dis­tor­tion of their own. In the early 1990s, Jagdish Bhagwati called it tar­iff-jumping FDI: for­eign­ers doing min­i­mal as­sem­bly of semi-knocked-down cars to sell be­hind the wall. Much of India’s car in­dus­try, Shah said, is like that. {111-C09}

~ Barriers raise the cost of in­puts too. Imported raw ma­te­ri­als for ar­ti­fi­cial fab­ric carry 10 per cent du­ties, Shah said, which make Indian yarn, cloth and shirts less com­pet­i­tive. {#tenpercent}

quote.text: So for the Indian rich, FDI is not in­ter­est­ing. FDI is not at­trac­tive be­cause it is com­pe­ti­tion for their own busi­nesses.

sections.label: Keeping faith
sections.head: Humble pie for the state
sections.caption: protecting foreign investors
body: Amit Varma re­called that when he first heard of SEZs, his “purest lib­er­tar­ian mind” asked why the whole coun­try should not be one, and reached for a line of verse: “Into that heaven of free­dom, my fa­ther, let my coun­try awake.” {111-J07}
His ques­tions were prac­ti­cal. How do you pro­tect for­eign­ers from a state he called “fun­da­men­tally a par­a­site for its own peo­ple”? And how do you give them pre­dictabil­ity?

China man­aged it, Ajay Shah said, with a trusted, pre­dictable mech­a­nism, until Xi Jinping: with a pop­ulist regime, all bets are off. Elsewhere, the an­swer is the bi­lat­eral in­vest­ment treaty, under which India com­pen­sates for­eign in­vestors it ex­pro­pri­ates.
## Team India

The union gov­ern­ment signs, so it must pay even when a state or city gov­ern­ment mis­be­haved. “We are team India,” Shah said. But front­line of­fi­cials de­tested pay­outs, and took lost cases per­son­ally, as bad for ca­reers and bud­gets.
Shah wants hu­mil­ity: ac­cept a slap in the face each time the state fum­bles, di­ag­nose what went wrong and fix it. {#slapped}
Instead, he said, the state turned ar­ro­gant: “It’s my sov­er­eign right to ex­pro­pri­ate you. How dare you tell me that I have to pay money.” {#sovereign}
~ Varma had a word for do­mes­tic firms. A level play­ing field mat­ters, he said, and he would fight for it. “But don’t deny this to for­eign firms.”

quote.text: The Indian state should get slapped in the face when the Indian state mis­be­haves.

sections.label: Graduation day
sections.head: Raju becomes a multinational
sections.caption: Indian firms going global
body: Amit Varma bor­rowed the chapter’s title from Aziz Mirza’s film *Raju Ban Gaya Gentleman*. He just likes the title, he said: Raju wants to be a gen­tle­man, and Indian firms want to be global firms. {111-J10}
Ajay Shah’s hope for India rests on its elite. The top end of the country’s knowl­edge spec­trum, he said, is “just out of the world”. {#elite}

The old third-worldism saw a de­vel­op­ing coun­try only as the help­less re­cip­i­ent of FDI. But in the last twenty years, Shah said, Indian firms have be­come multi­na­tion­als on a beau­ti­ful scale, some­thing unimag­in­able when he was young. He, Dilek Demirbas and Ila Patnaik wrote the first paper on it, *Graduating to Globalisation*.
## Up the lad­der

The Helpman-Melitz-Yeaple model ranks firms by pro­duc­tiv­ity: the weak­est stay do­mes­tic, bet­ter ones ex­port, the best do FDI abroad. Hundreds of Indian firms, Shah said, are now multi­na­tion­als. {#hundreds}

Indian soft­ware turns the lad­der up­side down. Firms that sit in India while for­eign busi­ness comes to them are the most pro­duc­tive; the body shop­pers who carry their peo­ple into the UK and Germany are weaker. {111-C12}
~ By that test, Shah said, this show has grad­u­ated too: 30 per cent of its au­di­ence is over­seas. {#audience}

quote.text: It’s up­side down that FDI Indian soft­ware com­pa­nies are worse than ex­port­ing Indian soft­ware com­pa­nies.

The magic of FDI is not in hav­ing for­eign com­pa­nies stand in line and be treated by Indian reg­u­la­tors and Indian cap­i­tal con­trols and Indian pass­port visa prob­lems, just like any­body else. Then what’s the point?

p3.title: Stories
p3.deck: Four tales of foreign investment welcomed, refused and driven away, and what each teaches

stories.kicker: Ajay Shah on how India and China drove investors away
stories.head: From Fernandes to Xi, a rerun
body: Ajay Shah’s sim­plest pic­ture of FDI is a for­eigner build­ing a fac­tory in India, and its sim­plest op­po­site is George Fernandes. Fernandes, he said, drove IBM and Coca-Cola out of India. {#fernandes1}
IBM had op­er­ated in India, sup­port­ing the IBM main­frames used here. Fernandes cre­ated con­di­tions under which it chose to pack its bags and leave. The same hap­pened to Coca-Cola.
The con­di­tions, as Shah de­scribed them, were the kind in­vestors dread: you will do tech­nol­ogy trans­fer into India, you will do an IPO in India, you will have a joint ven­ture in India.

China, for a while, went the other way. Deng Xiaoping ac­cepted that its in­sti­tu­tions were bad, and that fix­ing them would take a hun­dred years. Meanwhile he built a pre­dictable in­ter­face where the state left for­eign­ers alone. “Deng Xiaoping’s dream was there will be no Xi Jinping,” Shah said. {111-J02}
Then came Xi Jinping. Rules on tech­nol­ogy trans­fer and joint ven­tures crept back, Shah said: the same kind of con­di­tions Fernandes had im­posed in India. {111-S04}

“So this is the loss of clar­ity,” he said. There had been too much kind­ness in the way peo­ple spoke about FDI, and not enough in­tel­lec­tual clar­ity. The very rea­son the FDI-led model is so good, he said, is that it over­comes the fail­ure of do­mes­tic in­sti­tu­tions. Sure enough, FDI into China col­lapsed.
~ For how China came to this, Shah pointed lis­ten­ers to the hosts’ ear­lier episode *The China Model is Broken*. {111-R04}
stories.why: A country’s wel­come to for­eign cap­i­tal is not a per­ma­nent fea­ture. China’s, Shah sug­gested, rested on a po­lit­i­cal com­mit­ment to leave for­eign­ers alone, and the FDI went when the com­mit­ment did. {111-C03}

pic.caption: Ajay Shah on Fernandes, Deng and Xi

stories.kicker: Ajay Shah’s first brush with foreign investment
stories.head: Glass ceiling, made in India
body: In the early 1980s, Ajay Shah hap­pened to be around when an American from Corning Glass came to meet his fa­ther. Shah dates the visit by his father’s death in 1984.
Corning wanted to set up a fac­tory in India to make glass. It was a nice idea, Shah’s fa­ther agreed: there would be de­mand for such glass, for tele­vi­sion pic­ture tubes and so on.

But this is banned and that is banned, he told his guest, and the Indian state would ban it. The American was baf­fled that a gov­ern­ment would want to stop a com­pany build­ing fac­to­ries in its coun­try. {111-S01}
~ That was Shah’s first brush with FDI. Amit Varma re­framed it on the spot. “What you love is free­dom, isn’t it, Ajay?” he asked. {#freedom}

quote.text: And this guy was very baf­fled, why would the gov­ern­ment want to pre­vent us from build­ing fac­to­ries in India.

pic.caption: Ajay Shah on the man from Corning Glass

stories.kicker: Ajay Shah on a marquee investor that walked out
stories.head: Welcome mat, then the taxman
body: Nokia did ex­actly what India says it wants from for­eign com­pa­nies. It built a man­u­fac­tur­ing fa­cil­ity in Tamil Nadu.
Then, Ajay Shah said, “the Indian state went after them with in­come tax and freez­ing of as­sets and so on. And in the end, Nokia packed up and left.” {111-S02}

For Shah, the fail­ure was one of in­tel­lec­tual clar­ity. India lacked the dis­ci­pline to wall off the nor­mal depre­da­tions the state in­flicts on Indian com­pa­nies. Those, he said, “have to be kept out when you’re doing FDI”.

~ Otherwise there is noth­ing spe­cial about FDI. Indian en­trepreneurs are equally good and can buy for­eign tech­nol­ogy, and the coun­try faces a 200-year jour­ney to be­com­ing an ad­vanced econ­omy. {#twohundred}
stories.why: Inviting for­eign in­vestors is the easy half. Unless the state walls them off from the treat­ment it metes out to Indian firms, Shah ar­gued, even a mar­quee in­vest­ment can walk out. {111-C05}

pic.caption: Ajay Shah on Nokia’s exit from Tamil Nadu

stories.kicker: Ajay Shah on how knowledge leaves the factory gate
stories.head: Sewing the seeds in Bangladesh
body: Bangladesh’s gar­ment in­dus­try, in Ajay Shah’s telling, did not begin with Bangladeshi firms. Taiwanese and South Korean com­pa­nies came first and started gar­ment busi­nesses there. {111-S03}
Local peo­ple went to work for them and learned the trade. Then they stepped out and started gar­ment busi­nesses of their own, and the in­dus­try spread from there.

For Shah this is the ul­ti­mate prize of FDI. Workers in for­eign firms learn the global fron­tier of pro­duc­tiv­ity and how glob­alised pro­duc­tion works. That knowl­edge sits with them, not with the com­pany, and goes with them to other jobs and new firms. {111-C04}
~ “Again and again through world his­tory,” he said, “we have seen that knowl­edge dif­fu­sion hap­pen­ing.”
stories.why: If knowl­edge moves a so­ci­ety for­ward, the for­eign fac­tory is, in Shah’s word, the cru­cible where it is made. What it teaches walks out of the gate with its work­ers, into new jobs and new firms.

pic.caption: Ajay Shah on Bangladesh’s garment trade

overheard.text: FDI is lib­eral with her af­fec­tions. We do not have to com­pete. We can both get FDI.
overheard.who: Amit Varma, closing the episode’s love story

quiz.q: What equity stake did the OECD and IMF agree makes an investment FDI?
quiz.a: Ten per cent: a 9 per cent stake counts as port­fo­lio in­vest­ment.

quiz.q: How many FDI numbers does the balance of payments produce, by Ajay Shah’s count?
quiz.a: Seven: gross flows, repa­tri­a­tions and nets for each di­rec­tion, plus a ‘net net’.

quiz.q: Which foreign companies first set up garment businesses in Bangladesh, in Shah’s telling?
quiz.a: Taiwanese and South Korean com­pa­nies; their local staff later started firms of their own.

quiz.q: Who coined the phrase “tariff-jumping FDI”, and when did he raise it?
quiz.a: Jagdish Bhagwati, in the early 1990s, when India’s first FDI surge ar­rived.

quiz.q: Why does India’s business community welcome portfolio investment but resist FDI, according to Shah?
quiz.a: FDI means com­pe­ti­tion; port­fo­lio money means cheaper cap­i­tal. Ila Patnaik fig­ured it out.

quiz.q: In Indian software, which firms turned out less productive than pure exporters?
quiz.a: Those doing out­bound FDI by body shop­ping staff into the UK and Germany.

glossary.def: Foreign plants built only to get round a country’s trade bar­ri­ers.
Portfolio in­vest­ment feared be­cause it can buy today and sell to­mor­row.
A fa­cil­ity where im­ports enter and goods leave, ex­empt from the state.
Software firms car­ry­ing their of­fices and peo­ple into coun­tries like the UK.
Net FDI in India minus net FDI by India.
Bilateral in­vest­ment treaty: India pays the for­eign in­vestors it ex­pro­pri­ates.

p4.credits: Everything is Everything was Amit Varma and Ajay Shah’s weekly show, 128 episodes from June 2023 to December 2025. This edition is made from Episode 111. The moving pictures, stills and chapter cards are from its video; the chapter art is by Simahina. Every play button starts the video at the moment it was said. The articles and headlines were written by Claude, an AI model, from the episode’s machine-made transcript, and checked against it. Other photographs are from Wikimedia Commons: Jagdish Bhagwati (Johannes Jansson, CC BY 2.5 dk); Deng Xiaoping (Wikimedia Commons, public domain). The covers on the shelf are from Wikipedia.

shelf.title: Graduating to Globalisation (Episode 48)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
shelf.why: Ajay’s case that in­ter­na­tion­al­i­sa­tion is the en­gine of growth: com­pet­ing with the world forces firms to im­port best prac­tices and raise their game, and the gains spread through the econ­omy.

shelf.title: The Populist Playbook (Episode 42)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
shelf.why: Populism is not ‘what is popular’ but a dan­ger­ous pack­age of be­liefs and meth­ods, ris­ing world­wide along­side na­tion­al­ism, that works by in­vent­ing en­e­mies and sell­ing in­su­lar slo­gans like im­port sub­sti­tu­tion.

shelf.title: How to Do Development (Episode 57)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
shelf.why: The case, built on Lant Pritchett’s ev­i­dence, that every human wel­fare in­di­ca­tor tracks per capita GDP, so sus­tained growth, not re­dis­tri­bu­tion or small solv­able projects, is the way out of poverty.

shelf.title: The China Model is Broken (Episode 16)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
shelf.why: Why Chinese state con­trol and in­dus­trial pol­icy caused deep prob­lems be­hind the cherry-picked EV and solar suc­cesses: Xi’s cen­tral­i­sa­tion and na­tion­al­ism, cap­i­tal con­trols, real-estate over­build­ing, the exit of for­eign­ers and a failed eq­uity mar­ket.

shelf.title: What Ails Indian Manufacturing? (Episode 104)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
shelf.why: Ajay’s di­ag­no­sis of why Indian man­u­fac­tur­ing is weak: eight ways it dif­fers from ser­vices, twelve things that hob­ble it in India (from du­ties on im­ported in­puts to labour laws) and seven items for every state’s growth strat­egy.

shelf.title: Everything is Everything episode on the theory of change
shelf.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
shelf.why: The hosts’ the­ory of change: pol­icy im­proves through a decades-long pipe­line of data, re­search, rival pro­pos­als, pub­lic de­bate, com­mit­tee re­ports and draft laws, not by whis­per­ing in a joint secretary’s ear.

shelf.title: Inflation Targeting Rocks! (Episode 68)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
shelf.why: The full story of in­fla­tion tar­get­ing, which Ajay pushed for from the 1990s and which took more than fif­teen years to be­come law: a les­son in how slowly good pol­icy ar­rives.

shelf.title: How Family Firms Evolve (Episode 34)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
shelf.why: Original think­ing from Ajay on how Indian firms evolved over 30 years and how they should ma­ture: from fam­ily con­trol to dis­persed share­hold­ing, a pow­er­ful board and a man­age­ment team ac­count­able to it.

shelf.title: From Imperial to Adaptive Firms (Episode 37)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
shelf.why: How Indian firms moved from re­gional satraps in the 1980s to top-down ‘imperial’ firms with uni­form best prac­tices, and then to ‘adaptive’ firms that pair rules with local flex­i­bil­ity.

shelf.title: Going Bankrupt in India (Episode 80)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
shelf.why: Why bank­ruptcy is a healthy, nor­mal part of eco­nomic life, and how the pol­i­tics of India’s bank­ruptcy re­form gave big com­pa­nies out­sized in­flu­ence, left op­er­a­tional cred­i­tors weak and squeezed small manufacturers’ work­ing cap­i­tal.

shelf.title: How Much Wealth Do You Need to Retire? (Episode 110)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
shelf.why: Pointer to the pre­ced­ing episode in the se­ries.

shelf.title: Raju Ban Gaya Gentleman
shelf.creator: Aziz Mirza
shelf.why: Amit says he just likes the title: Raju wants to be a gen­tle­man, and Indian firms want to be global firms.

shelf.title: Graduating to Globalisation: A Study of Southern Multinationals
shelf.creator: Dilek Demirbas, Ila Patnaik and Ajay Shah
shelf.why: Ajay’s co-authored study of out­bound FDI by Indian firms that now build fac­to­ries and com­pa­nies abroad: a glo­ri­ous and often over­looked mode of in­ter­na­tion­al­i­sa­tion that was unimag­in­able when he was young.

shelf.title: Export Versus FDI in Services
shelf.creator: Rudrani Bhattacharya, Ila Patnaik and Ajay Shah
shelf.why: Ajay’s co-authored paper tak­ing the ex­port-versus-FDI ques­tion to ser­vices: in Indian soft­ware, firms that in­vest abroad are less pro­duc­tive than pure ex­porters, which turns the stan­dard in­ter­na­tion­al­i­sa­tion lad­der up­side down.

laughs.text: Amit opens by in­sist­ing ‘this episode is not about money, this episode is about love’. Ajay has con­fided five great loves: firm pro­duc­tiv­ity, cap­i­tal ac­count open­ness, in­fla­tion tar­get­ing and, above all, FDI. When Ajay says ‘in­fla­tion targeting’, Amit cracks, ‘Oh my God, you al­most came as you said that.’ He then asks, mock-romantically, ‘Tell me about the first time you guys met. You and FDI.’

After Ajay de­clares any­one who la­bels a chart just ‘FDI’ a pro­pa­gan­dist, Amit says: ‘You have ter­ri­fied me. I’m never gonna say FDI in front of you again. Straight away it will be like net in­flow, gross in­flow.’
Ajay ex­plains mar­ket churn with a for­eign seller matched by ‘a Bengali who is buying’. Amit quips: ‘Some for­eign port­fo­lio in­vestors are Bengali. We are ev­ery­where.’
Amit sums up the FDI-versus-FPI de­bate: ‘On one side of the de­bate you have se­cu­ri­ties. On the other side you have in­se­cu­ri­ties.’

Amit re­calls his first re­ac­tion to SEZs: ‘my purest lib­er­tar­ian mind re­acted by say­ing, Why do we need SEZ? A whole coun­try should be an SEZ. Into that heaven of free­dom, my fa­ther, let my coun­try awake.’ He caps it with a fa­mous line of verse.

Amit asks why there can’t be world-class Indian firms ‘when There are world class Indian YouTube shows’. Ajay de­clares the show ‘an ex­port­ing show’ with a 30% over­seas au­di­ence: ‘You have grad­u­ated.’ Amit pan­ics that this will in­vite an in­come-tax raid: ‘My head is spin­ning, bro.’
Raju Ban Gaya Gentleman (dir. Aziz Mirza) gives the chap­ter its title and metaphor: ‘Raju Wants to be gen­tle­men. Indian firms want to be global firms.’
The Vodafone ret­ro­spec­tive tax­a­tion episode, which Amit cites as the kind of ‘nonsense’ that de­stroys the pre­dictabil­ity for­eign in­vestors need.
Premier Padmini stands in for the pro­tected Indian in­cum­bent threat­ened by a for­eigner mak­ing cars in India. Indian retail’s anger at Amazon and Walmart is the mod­ern ver­sion.
